chapters.title: 1. Finite bandits, traces, and regret
chapters.summary: The deterministic language shared by the entire project: finite models, action and reward traces, pull counts, gaps, reward sums, pseudo-regret, and count-to-regret decompositions.
chapters.audience: Start here if you know basic probability or machine learning but are new to this Lean library.
learning_goals: Distinguish a deterministic action trace from a probability law over generated traces.
Use pull counts as the bookkeeping interface shared by ETC, UCB, EXP3, and Tsallis routes.
Read the finite-sum identity that regroups time-indexed regret by arm.
open_gaps: The deterministic identities are reusable; each probabilistic algorithm still needs its own measurable generated law and integrability contracts.
A local model-facing endpoint need not match every textbook or upstream theorem signature.

chapters.title: 2. Probability, kernels, filtrations, and concentration
chapters.summary: Measure-theoretic infrastructure for generated histories, conditional reward laws, martingale differences, posterior kernels, stopping times, and concentration.
chapters.audience: Read after Foundations; familiarity with conditional expectation helps but is not required.
learning_goals: See why policies and history selectors must be measurable maps.
Separate a marginal reward distribution from a history-conditioned kernel law.
Track adaptedness, integrability, finite-measure, and variance-proxy assumptions explicitly.
open_gaps: Strong conditional-law and stopping-time adapters compile, but there is no single producer for every adaptive environment.
Self-normalized and RL-specific concentration remain explicit theorem routes rather than one universal wrapper.

chapters.title: 3. Explore-Then-Commit
chapters.summary: Round-robin exploration, empirical means, measurable commit choices, wrong-commit tails, and expected-regret assemblies under bounded or sub-Gaussian arm laws.
chapters.audience: The shortest end-to-end stochastic-bandit route in the repository.
learning_goals: Decompose regret into deterministic exploration cost and wrong-commit probability.
Follow empirical-mean concentration into a concrete Real expected-regret bound.
Distinguish compiled local endpoints from the still-partial upstream-compatible port.
open_gaps: Direct LML integration remains cross-toolchain work even though concrete local ETC endpoints compile.
The website never upgrades a theorem card into a local proof certificate.

chapters.title: 4. UCB: confidence events to regret
chapters.summary: History-based UCB scores, count thresholds, generated policies, arm streams, finite-arm and context-dependent reward kernels, expected regret, and asymptotic consistency.
chapters.audience: Read ETC first if confidence-event arguments are new to you.
learning_goals: Convert a suboptimal UCB selection into a confidence failure or a small-count event.
Trace conditional sub-Gaussian laws into a textbook-shaped gap-sum bound.
Read the compiled expected-average-regret convergence results without conflating them with every UCB variant.
open_gaps: Multiple local UCB laws and asymptotic consumers compile; exact compatibility with the pinned upstream LML declaration remains a separate task.
KL-UCB confidence inversion is not supplied by the ordinary UCB route.

chapters.title: 5. OFUL, self-normalized confidence, and stopping times
chapters.summary: Elliptical potential, Gaussian-mixture self-normalization, ridge confidence, strict measurable optimistic selection, finite-window and all-time regret, expected rates, and random-horizon consumers.
chapters.audience: Read the Probability layer and UCB chapter before this linear-bandit route.
learning_goals: Understand the log-determinant proof of the elliptical-potential inequality.
Follow a conditional MGF source through ridge confidence and optimistic action selection.
Separate deterministic horizons, simultaneous one-policy confidence, and square-integrable stopping-time conclusions.
open_gaps: The repository now contains explicit finite-window expected rates, fixed-model average-regret consistency, one-policy all-time confidence, and stopping-time theorems; broader contextual, dynamic, and minimax claims remain separate.
Budget-forced schedules compile under explicit contracts, but this is not a full primal-dual Bandits-with-Knapsacks theorem.

chapters.title: 6. Thompson sampling and Bayesian regret
chapters.summary: Posterior kernels, conditional action-law identities, trajectory construction, clipped-UCB decomposition, and stationary latent-arm-stream regret.
chapters.audience: Best read after the Probability layer.
learning_goals: Read a posterior as a kernel from histories to environments.
Transport conditional action-law equality onto the generated trajectory.
Understand why one compiled stationary theorem is not a universal posterior-sampling result.
open_gaps: The stationary latent-arm-stream endpoint is compiled; broader posterior models need their own law producers.
Exact upstream compatibility remains an independently tracked task.

chapters.title: 7. EXP3 and adversarial concentration
chapters.summary: Exponential-weight potentials, importance weighting, generated trajectories, expected and high-probability regret, variance-sensitive refinements, and sparse-loss routes.
chapters.audience: Read Foundations first; later sections use the Probability layer heavily.
learning_goals: Connect the one-step exponential-potential inequality to deterministic Hedge regret.
See why positive exploration makes importance-weighted estimators legal.
Track predictable variance and sparsity failures into explicit probability events.
open_gaps: Expected, realized, Bernstein, predictable-variance, and sparse-loss endpoints compile under different exact hypotheses; there is no single hypothesis-free EXP3 theorem.
The declaration catalog, not historical route-card prose, is authoritative for current local code.

chapters.title: 8. Tsallis-FTRL, corruption, and nonstationarity
chapters.summary: Half-Tsallis stability, generated schedules, self-bounding interpolation, corruption bounds, IID and nonidentical reward laws, dynamic comparators, switch counts, and a generated oracle-restart route.
chapters.audience: This is one of the longest routes; read EXP3 and the Probability layer first.
learning_goals: Separate deterministic FTRL stability from stochastic law transport.
Use expected action probabilities and gap self-bounds to obtain logarithmic or corruption-sensitive regret.
Follow the now-compiled generated oracle-restart law while preserving its full-information change-point assumption.
open_gaps: Model-specific logarithmic, refined, dynamic, and oracle-restart endpoints compile, but complete literature-level Tsallis-INF with paper-sharp constants is not claimed.
The oracle restart uses population-mean change points; an observed-reward detector would require a random history-dependent schedule plus concentration for delay and false alarms.

chapters.title: 9. Finite-horizon reinforcement learning
chapters.summary: Finite MDPs, Markov policies, Bellman optimality, generated trajectories, occupancy-regret identities, empirical model confidence, adaptive cumulative exploration, realized behavior regret, consistency, and genuine hittingAfter stopping times.
chapters.audience: Read Foundations, Probability, UCB, and the OFUL stopping-time material first.
learning_goals: Build finite-horizon value recursion and prove the optimal policy attains the Bellman optimum.
Rewrite expected policy regret as an occupancy-weighted Bellman gap.
Follow adaptive empirical confidence through realized behavior consistency and fixed-index stopped expected-regret bounds.
open_gaps: The RL layer is no longer planned: hundreds of declarations compile, including stochastic reward, adaptive cumulative, causal, consistency, and stopping-time routes.

The current terminal is not complete UCB-VI: raw-episode regret, behavior=recommended equality, arbitrary-MDP reachability, minimax rates, optional stopping, uniform-in-threshold integrability, and L1 convergence remain explicit boundaries.

chapters.title: 10. Automation, resources, and open routes
chapters.summary: The proof harness, task vocabulary, resource stopping leaves, literature registry, and planned KL-UCB, BwK, preference, robust, delayed, federated, and neural-bandit work.
chapters.audience: Read this chapter to contribute a new route or understand what is deliberately not claimed.
learning_goals: Use the same status vocabulary for source declarations, theorem cards, tasks, and blockers.
Distinguish a stopping-time foundation from a completed resource-constrained algorithm theorem.
Move a literature target through task packets, proof obligations, compilation, and synchronized documentation.
open_gaps: KL-UCB, full BwK/primal-dual regret, dueling, robust/delayed, federated, and neural-bandit routes remain planned or partial unless a named local declaration says otherwise.
The harness records completion gates but does not replace Lean elaboration or mathematical review.
